rv.q: Perhaps this ‘Camelot’ is a manifestation practice for Sorkin, one that bolsters egalitarian rulers who value love and mercy just as highly as power and might...Genial heroes are needed to move us forward.
The revival makes you want to believe in a great musical called Camelot, even if such a thing never did exist.
It doesn't, though there are a few flashes that throw enough illumination to let us see where he was going.
What remains is a cooler “Camelot,” with its own head-scratching dramaturgy.
It moves like a funeral procession for itself.
What this unhappy queen truly wants is the one intriguingly unsettled mystery in a “Camelot” that conjures anything but wonder.
Neither, it seems, is sufficient today.
It’s the chilliest “Camelot” you ever did see and it embodies so many of the current neuroses surrounding the revival of classic American musicals.
Camelot is a sweeping drama packed with royal romance and sword fights.

Reinvigorated by Sorkin — who has long painted a dreamy, egalitarian view of politics within his works — and his new book, the musical succeeds in evoking that dream for one brief, shining moment once again.
Indeed, this Camelot, which I admittedly could not muster up much enthusiasm for upon entering the Theater, was surprisingly engaging.

If this Camelot is a bit confused on whether it wants to be a majestic golden age musical or a gritty take on the shaky foundations of a monarchical ménage à trois, it pulls through on the strength of its cast, which tightly brings the work’s brief shining moment into glorious light.
And magic is exactly what this Camelot most obviously lacks.

“Sorkin eventually hands us a somewhat shocking revelation about five minutes before the show is over, which if it had been spoken aloud (or hinted at more broadly earlier) would absolutely have deepened the show and given it the spark it needed to ignite.
So smoothed out has the story become that the actors – admirable all – can do little more than stay afloat.
But, as entertaining as the musical numbers are, it’s hard not to be disappointed by this production.
Ultimately, though, this Camelot revival falls on its own sword with its reworked book.
It’s a shame that this “Camelot,” despite its shining moments and impeccable pedigree, doesn’t offer more of that kind of splendor.
It’s seldom exciting or joyful.
For what it’s worth, all this talk of love in the final scene came as news to me.

Unfortunately, his new book (which removes all magical elements, turns Morgan Le Fey as a scientist, and questions how Arthur could have pulled the sword from the stone) is too clumsy and self-conscious in its attempt to draw contemporary parallels and critical viewpoints.
It is to be hoped that future musical revivals of golden age shows will either trust the original material or their audiences to know that things were different in earlier decades.
Due to Sorkin’s undernourished scribing, the emotions the songs reveal don’t fit the emotion-deprived characters.
Camelot remains as disjointed as before.
The result is arid, a musical that can't decide why anyone is singing.
At almost three hours on a spartan stage, it grinds into a numbingly boring show.
The result is Sorkin’s retrofitted play, where mostly incongruous songs with erudite lyrics infrequently pop in.
Sorkin's book and stunning lead performances make this truly next level.
Still, I'm afraid most of the blame for this revisal's failings have to be laid at Sorkin's door.

cn.t: Critics find this revival of "Camelot" a disappointing slog, with Sorkin's magic-free rewrite draining the color and romance from Lerner and Loewe's score. While Soo's vocals and the orchestra earn praise, the production feels gloomy and overlong.

vs.sum: The Vivian Beaumont Theater offers exceptional sightlines and sound quality due to its unique thrust stage design, ensuring a great view and auditory experience from nearly every seat. While the ambiance is enhanced by its location within the Lincoln Center, the comfort level is average with some reports of tight seating, and facilities are typical for a Broadway venue.

acc.note: Orchestra accessible via elevator. Induction hearing loop for t-coil. Loge NOT accessible (stairs only).
